articles.headline: Fed Holds Rates, Then Sends Two Officials to Explain Why It Will Not Hold Rates
articles.dek: Two regional Fed presidents said more hikes are coming, hours after the committee held steady and its chairman declined to say what he planned to do.
articles.catch_up: The Federal Reserve left interest rates unchanged on Wednesday, a month after raising them for the first time since 2023. Two of its officials dissented in favor of a hike, and Chairman Kevin Warsh announced plans to cancel rate votes at three future meetings.
articles.why_it_matters: If the Fed raises rates again, borrowing costs for mortgages, car loans and business credit stay higher for longer, with inflation near 3.7% and unemployment at 4.2%. Fewer scheduled rate votes also means fewer clues about when those costs will change.
body: The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday. By Friday, two of its regional presidents were publicly explaining that rates will need to go up, according to CNBC. Nothing says a pause quite like a speaking tour about the end of the pause.

St. Louis Fed President Alberto Musalem said "additional firming of monetary policy will be necessary, and soon." Translation: firming means raising rates, a word chosen because it sounds like something that happens to a mattress. Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan went further, saying the committee needs at least two more quarter-point increases. A quarter point, or 25 basis points, is the standard unit of Fed adjustment, small enough to be called gradual and large enough to appear on your mortgage statement.

Logan added that skipping a meeting does not change the destination, which is a reassuring thing to say about a road trip that has apparently lost a few exits. Traders took the hint: CME's FedWatch tool put the odds of a quarter-point hike in December at about 76%, according to CNBC.

The case for acting is fairly plain. Musalem called the economy resilient. GDP grew 3.4%, unemployment is 4.2%, and the personal consumption expenditures index, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, showed annual inflation above 3%. The Fed's target is 2%. Latest consumer price data show inflation at 3.74%, which is not near 2% by any generous reading of the word near. Fed funds sit at 3.88%, and the 10-year Treasury yields 4.98%, so markets are already charging more for long money than the Fed is for overnight money.

Two voting members, Governor Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, wanted a hike this week and dissented. Former Richmond Fed President Jeffrey Lacker said he was surprised by the lack of urgency, given inflation near three to three-and-a-half percent for so long.

Why, then, did the Fed hold? CNBC's analysis suggests Warsh prefers to keep Wall Street guessing. He said that if the Fed had a firm conclusion, it would announce it with fanfare. He also said financial conditions are tighter, but that he is unwilling and unable to call them tight. Translation: it is a hike in a trench coat, not yet ready to be seen in public.

Before the meeting, a pair of top officials appeared to talk down expectations of a hike. Warsh declined to say he sent them, remarking that he is not some all-knowing person sending messages out. CNBC notes that this gives him plausible deniability, a feature that no central bank has ever listed in its mandate but most have used.

Warsh also announced that one meeting in 2027 and two in 2028 will focus on broader strategy, with no rate decision or statement expected. The Fed will still meet eight times a year. Critics are unimpressed. Former St. Louis Fed President James Bullard warned that a volatile world might force a special meeting anyway. Lacker suggested the opposite remedy: if you want less pressure on each meeting, hold more of them. MarketWatch framed the dispute as a chairman who wants the Fed to say less against officials pushing for more transparency.

PGIM economist Robert Sockin called the hold a policy mistake, arguing that a gradual Fed may have to hike higher later, raising recession risk. Warsh's defenders say the data due before December will settle things, and could even show productivity rising enough to permit growth without inflation.
The next meeting is in December. Until then, the most reliable forecasting tool at the Fed is the schedule of speeches by people who say they do not speak for the chairman.
articles.wire_headline: Fed officials are already saying they’ll need to get back to hiking rates

articles.headline: Economy Grows 3.4% While Prices Also Grow, Fed Promises to Keep Looking at Both
articles.dek: Third-quarter GDP beat forecasts and layoffs stayed near 1960s lows, but September inflation hit 3.6% a day after the Fed held rates steady.
articles.catch_up: The Commerce Department reported Thursday that GDP grew at a 3.4% annualized pace in the third quarter, while its preferred inflation gauge rose 0.5% in September. The Fed had voted a day earlier to hold its benchmark rate at 3.75%-4%.
articles.why_it_matters: Strong growth combined with inflation well above the Fed's 2% target makes rate cuts harder to justify, which affects mortgage, loan and savings rates. Energy costs, which jumped in September, hit household budgets directly.
body: The U.S. economy grew faster than economists expected from July through September, according to Commerce Department figures reported by CNBC. GDP rose at a seasonally adjusted annualized pace of 3.4%, against a forecast of 3.1% and 2.2% in the second quarter. The same morning, the government reported that inflation was also doing well, in the sense that it was still there.

Translation: annualized means the quarter's pace is projected across a full year, so the economy did not literally grow 3.4% in three months. It grew at a speed that would produce 3.4% if it kept going. Economists use this convention because it makes every number look like a different, larger number.

The inflation figures came from the personal consumption expenditures price index, the Fed's favored gauge. Prices rose 0.5% in September, the biggest monthly rise since March, taking the annual rate to 3.6%, a tenth below forecasts. Excluding food and energy, the so-called core measure rose 0.3% on the month and 3.1% over the year, in line with expectations. Translation: core strips out the items people actually buy most often, on the theory that it shows the underlying trend more clearly.

Energy was the culprit. Gasoline and other energy goods rose 9.2% in September, and energy goods and services overall climbed 5.4%. Economists, CNBC noted, fear this could spread to other parts of the economy. Services excluding energy and housing rose 0.4%, and housing costs rose 0.3%. Brent crude was most recently listed at $123.10 a barrel.

There was some mild good news. Measured quarterly, headline PCE prices rose 2.1% and core prices 2.5%, down from 5% and 3.3% in the second quarter. The quarterly figure says prices behaved better across the summer, and the monthly one says September did not get the memo.

Growth is being driven largely by the artificial intelligence build-out and by consumers and government. Consumer spending rose 3.8% in the quarter, and private domestic investment soared 19.4%, with equipment spending up 20.9% and intellectual property products up 8.4%. Real sales to private domestic purchasers, which the Fed treats as a gauge of underlying demand, rose 4.9%. Translation: nobody is slowing down, which is wonderful news for growth and a headache for anyone trying to cool prices.

The labor market offered no relief either. Initial jobless claims fell to 194,000 for the week ended Oct. 24, below the 200,000 estimate and near levels last seen in the late 1960s. Chris Rupkey of Fwdbonds said growth is "powering ahead" despite geopolitical risks and higher energy costs.

All of this landed one day after the Fed held its benchmark rate at 3.75%-4%. Chairman Kevin Warsh said Wednesday that "the period right in front of us is information rich." CNBC observed that Thursday's data deluge suggests the Fed could have more work to do. Futures fell and Treasury yields slipped after the releases. The 10-year yield stood at 4.98% on Wednesday, and the Fed's next meeting will reveal how much information is too much.
articles.wire_headline: Third-quarter U.S. GDP increases a better-than-expected 3.4% as September inflation accelerates

articles.headline: ECB Holds Rates at 2.5%, Then Lagarde Announces She Would Like to Speak Freely
articles.dek: The central bank paused at 2.5% despite 3.8% inflation, and its president said she will leave in February 2027 to gain the freedom to say things.
articles.catch_up: The European Central Bank raised rates in June for the first time since 2023 and again in September, as energy prices rose following the outbreak of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran in February. On Thursday it held its deposit rate at 2.5%, and Christine Lagarde announced her early exit.
articles.why_it_matters: Euro zone borrowers face higher financing costs while the ECB weighs another hike in December, and the next president will inherit a French bond market under strain. Whoever gets the job will decide how far the bank goes to defend a currency shared by 21 countries.
body: The European Central Bank voted on Thursday to leave its key interest rate, the deposit facility, at 2.5%, as markets expected, according to CNBC. Euro zone inflation reached 3.8% last month, a three-year high. The bank has therefore responded to a three-year inflation high by doing nothing, which in central banking counts as a firm statement.

The Governing Council said rising energy prices threaten to push inflation up and growth down, while underlying inflation and wages have so far been broadly stable. Energy price inflation hit 18.8%. Translation: the things that are expensive are expensive for obvious reasons, and the ECB would like to see whether they make everything else expensive too.

Christine Lagarde said the council debated a hike and then decided unanimously to hold. She said the bank is not seeing "second round effects", which means companies and workers have not yet responded to pricier energy by raising prices and demanding higher pay. That is the behavior central banks fear most, and they prefer to watch for it rather than cause it.

Lagarde pointed to two developments since the last meeting: higher energy costs and a sharp rise in long-term financing costs, with the average 10-year sovereign yield up about 35 basis points. Translation: a basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, so 35 of them is a third of a percent, which is a lot when governments owe trillions. She also blamed part of the rise on bond issuance by hyperscalers, the large tech companies building AI infrastructure, who are competing with governments for the same lenders.

Money markets, according to LSEG data, priced about a 67% chance of a hike in December. Deutsche Bank's Mark Wall expects one, to 2.75%, and calls it probably the end of the cycle. UBS's Dean Turner called Thursday's decision a "hawkish pause". Translation: the bank is stopping to catch its breath, not to put its feet up.

Then came the larger news. Lagarde will step down on Feb. 7 next year, nearly nine months before her term ends in October 2027. She said she wants the freedom of speech to engage on matters that are not monetary policy, because ECB presidents must stay neutral. She said she cannot remain comfortable in that neutrality at present. She did not name the matters, which is consistent with the neutrality she is leaving to escape.

The timing has consequences. Her exit falls before the French presidential election, where CNBC reports polling suggests Marine Le Pen is the frontrunner. Aberdeen's Felix Feather noted the new French president will have no role in choosing the next ECB head. Appointments are made by the European Council after consulting the European Parliament and euro area states, so the independent central bank is chosen by politicians, as is traditional.

The reported leading candidates are Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos and the Netherlands' Klaas Knot. Analysts cited by CNBC see Knot as more hawkish, meaning more inclined to raise rates, and De Cos as more continuity-minded. Berenberg's Holger Schmieding said the ECB has no mandate and no appetite to fund French fiscal follies, which is a notable thing to say about a country whose bond spread over Germany is at its highest since the early 2010s sovereign debt crisis.

Chief economist Philip Lane and board member Isabel Schnabel are also due to leave next year. The bank is therefore preparing to replace much of its leadership while inflation is high and France is borrowing at rising costs. Lagarde, for her part, got a standing ovation. Whether anyone listens to what she says next, as she put it, is another story.
articles.wire_headline: European Central Bank keeps key interest rate on hold at 2.5%

articles.headline: Exxon and Chevron Post Record Highs as the World Runs Short of Diesel
articles.dek: Both oil majors beat estimates on third-quarter profits of $15.4 billion and $9.9 billion, as wars in Iran and Ukraine squeeze refining capacity.
articles.catch_up: Fuel supplies have been disrupted since March, when the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran and Tehran began striking ships in the Strait of Hormuz. Attacks by Ukraine, Iran and Houthi militants on refineries in Russia and the Middle East have cut global refining capacity further, CNBC reported.
articles.why_it_matters: Diesel moves freight, farm equipment and construction, so a 70% jump in its price shows up in the cost of nearly everything else. The same shortage that strains household budgets is what is producing the record corporate profits.
body: ExxonMobil and Chevron reported sharply higher third-quarter profits on Friday, and both stocks touched all-time highs, CNBC reported. Exxon's profit doubled to $15.4 billion from $7.5 billion a year earlier. Chevron's net income rose nearly 200% to $9.9 billion. Both companies beat Wall Street estimates, which is a feat when the quarter's main event is a global fuel emergency.

The cause is simple. Refineries in Russia and the Middle East have been hit by Ukrainian, Iranian and Houthi attacks, removing millions of barrels per day of capacity. Importers have turned to U.S. Gulf Coast refineries, which belong in large part to companies like these two. Exxon's Gulf Coast plants ran at 100% capacity. Chevron's U.S. refineries ran at 98% and processed just over 1 million barrels a day, a record.

Translation: when nobody else can make diesel, the people who still can get to name the price. Chevron's refining profit rose more than 300% to $4.9 billion. Exxon's refining arm earned about $7.2 billion in the quarter, narrowly beating its production business at about $7.1 billion. In other words, the part of the company that turns oil into fuel is now worth more than the part that finds the oil.

Exxon CEO Darren Woods told CNBC that diesel is the key crunch point because demand is very inelastic. Translation: people buy it at any price because trucks cannot run on optimism. AAA put the U.S. national average at $6.32 a gallon on Friday, up more than 70% from a year ago, after a record high in September.

Chevron CEO Mike Wirth said the system is under stress and the environment is fairly fragile. This is an unusual thing for the owner of a record-setting refinery to say, but it is also the business case. Fragility is what the quarterly results are made of.

Production did not share in the fun. Chevron's oil and gas output slipped to 3.9 million barrels a day from about 4 million, partly because of the conflict in the Middle East. Exxon has produced about 4.5 million barrels a day this year, down more than 2%. The profit comes from scarcity, not from pumping more.

The politics are awkward. CNBC noted that President Donald Trump said in August that the two companies were making too much money based on a shortage. Friday's numbers suggest the companies heard him and made even more.

The shipping picture explains why this may last. A second CNBC report said tankers are still moving crude through Hormuz despite a record number of attacks in October. At least 30 vessels were hit this month, according to the International Maritime Organization, and Brent traded above $117 on Friday. Ships are using a shuttle system, with transponders off, that pushed supertanker rates above $900,000 a day in early October. It works only because of U.S. air cover, and no one is sure how long Washington will stay engaged after Tuesday's midterms.
Watch whether the shuttle system holds and whether Congress changes the war's direction. If it does, diesel could get cheaper. Refiners would then have to find a new way to explain the record year.
articles.wire_headline: Chevron and Exxon hit all-time highs as refining profits soar in reaction to Iran and Ukraine wars
